title: How should passwords be stored and verified?
description: Adaptive salted KDFs (PBKDF2, bcrypt, Argon2), why encryption is wrong, and login-abuse defenses.

data.text: **Question:** How should passwords be stored and verified?

With a **slow, salted password-hashing function** — PBKDF2, bcrypt, scrypt, or Argon2 — not encryption and not a fast hash. Salts are random per user and stored alongside the hash so identical passwords don't produce identical digests and rainbow tables die. Verification recomputes the hash with the stored parameters and compares in **constant time**. Fast hashes (MD5, SHA-256) are for integrity, not passwords: a GPU guesses billions per second.

**Why hashing instead of encryption:**
- Encryption must be reversible with a key — a leaked key or backup exposes every password
- The server only ever needs "does this input match?" — one-way by design

**What a good password hash provides:**
- **Slowness (key stretching):** iterations/work factor calibrated so one verification takes ~100ms–1s on server hardware — attacker throughput collapses at scale
- **Unique salt per user:** generated with a CSPRNG, stored in the record (it is not secret); kills rainbow tables and precomputation
- **Future-proof parameters:** store algorithm + iterations/memory/parallelism *in the hash string* so you can raise cost and re-hash lazily on next login
- **Constant-time comparison** to avoid timing side channels

**Choices:**
- **PBKDF2** — built into .NET (`Rfc2898DeriveBytes`, HMAC-SHA256/512); FIPS-friendly; needs high iteration counts (OWASP: 600k+ for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256)
- **bcrypt** — battle-tested, cost factor built in; fixed 72-byte password limit
- **Argon2id** — modern winner (memory-hard, resists GPU/ASIC attacks); OWASP first choice when available
- ASP.NET Core Identity ships PBKDF2 with format versioning (v2/v3) and transparent re-hash on parameter upgrade

**Around the hash:** rate-limit/log failed logins, block credential stuffing (breed-list checks), never reveal "user doesn't exist" vs "wrong password", and store the password **verbatim** — no silent truncation, upper-casing, or unicode 'normalization' surprises

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Salt vs pepper vs iteration count — and why each exists
- Knowing fast hashes are wrong for passwords, and encryption is worse
- Practicality: where parameters live, how upgrades happen (lazy re-hash on login)
- The surrounding controls: rate limiting, enumeration, breach checking

items: MD5/SHA-256 with a salt — salted but still fast; brute-forceable on GPUs
One global salt shared by all users instead of a random one per record
Encrypting passwords — a key compromise reverses the entire table
Hard-coded iteration counts with no versioning, making future cost increases painful
Revealing account existence through different login error messages
Silently truncating passwords (old limits) or transforming case/content on signup
What is a pepper and where does it live if not in the database?
How would you upgrade PBKDF2 iterations for millions of existing users?
How does a breach-corpus check (k-anonymity) work without sending the password?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use an adaptive KDF: Argon2id, bcrypt, scrypt, or PBKDF2 with high iterations
Random per-user salt, stored with the hash; parameters stored in the record
Constant-time verification; never encrypt or fast-hash passwords
Layer login defenses: rate limits, uniform errors, breach checks
data.takeaway: Passwords need slow, salted, parameterized hashing — designed so a database leak stays expensive for the attacker.
